title: Physical Simulation - Particles, Wind, Volumes, Water, Cloth, and Collision
abstract: A mechanics-first guide to particles, wind, fog, clouds, water and oceans, fire and explosions, cloth and fibers, and the full collision pipeline—with equations, primary sources, and current AI research.
image: /content/blog/Physical Simulation - Particles, Wind, Volumes, Water, Cloth, and Collision/physical-simulation.svg
imageAlt: A particle stream crosses wind and cloud fields, becomes an ocean wave and fire plume, drapes into cloth, and reaches a collision boundary
lede: Physical simulation turns authored state into motion by advancing conservation laws, forces, constraints, phase changes, and contacts through time. This guide follows eight production-scale domains without pretending one solver fits all of them. Every keyword has a short definition, an equation where it adds information, an honest AI-research note, and a shared source group only when the same papers or documentation truly support the concepts together.

sections.heading: Particle simulation: state, integration, and constraints
paragraphs: A particle is a compact moving state, not a rendering primitive. Its position, velocity, mass, age, and custom attributes are advanced by forces or constraints; a separate renderer later chooses sprites, meshes, ribbons, strands, or volume splats.

The practical loop is spawn, accumulate forces, integrate, solve constraints and collisions, retire dead particles, then publish the state to rendering. A fixed or carefully bounded time step is essential because a visually plausible emitter can still become numerically unstable when frame time changes.

sections.heading: Wind: a velocity field coupled to objects
paragraphs: Wind is best represented as a time-varying velocity field. A procedural gust is sufficient for foliage or particles; smoke, sails, and dense crowds need spatial variation, turbulence, and a coupling law that converts relative air motion into drag and lift.

Grid solvers advect velocity, add viscosity and forces, and project the result to remove divergence. Artists often layer divergence-free noise and moving gust envelopes over a coarse flow because a fully resolved atmospheric simulation is rarely affordable.

sections.heading: Fog: transported density in a participating medium
paragraphs: Fog simulation produces a density field; fog rendering converts that field into extinction and in-scattered light. Keeping those responsibilities separate matters: advection, diffusion, buoyancy, sources, and dissipation evolve the medium, while the renderer integrates transmittance along camera and light rays.

An Eulerian grid is natural for broad fog banks and smoke-like motion. Sparse volume storage avoids allocating empty space, and a simulation-to-render handoff records density, temperature, velocity, and optional emission without baking lighting into the physical state.

sections.heading: Clouds: moisture, temperature, and phase change
paragraphs: A cloud is not only noise. A compact physical model transports water vapor and temperature, condenses vapor when local humidity exceeds saturation, evaporates cloud water when air becomes undersaturated, and feeds latent heat back into buoyancy.

Games often combine a coarse weather map with procedural detail because cloud microphysics spans scales that cannot be resolved in real time. The useful division is physical fields for evolution and coverage, then shaped noise for sub-grid structure—not noise pretending to be the entire simulation.

sections.heading: Water and ocean: free surfaces across scales
paragraphs: Water methods are chosen by scale. Spectral FFT oceans and Gerstner waves describe kilometers of deep-water surface efficiently; shallow-water equations capture coastlines and height-field flow; SPH and particle-in-cell families handle splashes, breaking waves, and strongly changing topology.

No single representation covers the whole shot. A practical ocean couples a large spectral surface to local free-surface simulation, then seeds foam and spray from curvature, vorticity, or breaking-wave criteria. Conservation and boundary exchange are more important than hiding the seam with extra noise.

sections.heading: Fire and explosion: reacting flow and pressure
paragraphs: Fire is a reacting flow: fuel and oxidizer create heat and products, hot gas rises, soot carries visible emission, and radiation loses energy. An explosion adds a rapid energy release that can produce compressible flow, a shock front, and a pressure impulse before the later buoyant plume behaves more like ordinary fire and smoke.

Entertainment solvers often simplify chemistry into progress variables and artist controls. That is reasonable when the model keeps its bookkeeping clear: reaction consumes fuel, heat changes temperature and density, soot is transported, and an explosion's early pressure wave is not confused with a slow incompressible plume.

sections.heading: Cloth and fiber: shells, yarns, and contact
paragraphs: Cloth is a thin anisotropic structure: it resists stretching strongly, shears differently along warp and weft, bends easily, and develops detail through contact. Triangle-shell, FEM, mass–spring, PBD, and XPBD models approximate those energies at different cost and controllability.

Fiber or yarn-level simulation moves below the homogenized sheet and resolves interlocking loops and friction. It produces characteristic knit and weave behavior, but requires much more geometry and collision work. Most real-time systems therefore use shell dynamics plus material parameters measured or tuned for the fabric.

sections.heading: Collision: broad phase, intersection, and push out
paragraphs: Collision handling is a pipeline. The broad phase rejects obviously separated pairs with cheap bounding volumes; the narrow phase computes actual separation or penetration; continuous collision detection checks motion between frames; the response stage applies impulses, friction, or positional correction.

AABB and k-DOP are not competing full solvers. They are bounding volumes used to organize candidate tests, often inside a BVH. Push out is a positional repair based on contact normal and penetration depth; it should complement velocity response, not silently replace time-of-impact handling.

aiResearch.summary: Recent differentiable collision work focuses on stable gradients through contact, while few-shot neural simulators learn local contact behavior from sparse examples. Geometry-based broad and narrow phases remain essential for coverage and safety.

closing: Particles provide moving samples; wind and volumetric solvers transport fields; clouds add phase change; oceans connect spectra to local free surfaces; fire couples reaction and flow; cloth turns thin-material energy into folds; collision keeps every representation mutually consistent. Modern AI is most useful as an inverse model, asset generator, or surrogate around these mechanisms—not as a reason to stop defining state, units, boundaries, conservation, and contact.
